title: Ilam Tea Garden Travel Guide: Kanyam to Antu Danda
meta_description: Ilam tea garden travel guide: how to get there from Siliguri and Kathmandu, Kanyam, Antu Danda sunrise, Mai Pokhari, tea seasons, itineraries and costs.
summary: Ilam, Nepal's oldest tea district, is about 3 hours from the Kakarbhitta border or Bhadrapur airport. Two to four nights cover the Kanyam slopes, the Ilam Bazaar estate, Mai Pokhari lake and sunrise over Kanchenjunga from Antu Danda. October–April gives clear views; March–May the first flush. Our 5-day tour costs from ₹22,000.

sections.heading: Why Ilam is different from Darjeeling
paras: Ilam sits on the same ridges as Darjeeling, just across the Mechi River and the Singalila range, and grows tea in much the same climate. Nepal's tea industry began here around 1863, when Colonel Gajraj Singh Thapa planted the Ilam and Soktim estates. Today the hills of Ilam, Kanyam, Fikkal and Antu produce orthodox leaf teas, mostly sold abroad, while the flat gardens of Jhapa below grow the CTC tea that goes into Nepal's milk tea.

What sets Ilam apart for visitors is how quiet it is. There are no toy trains or crowded malls; the bazaar at about 1,200 m is a working hill town of shops, dairies and tea traders. You walk among the bushes freely, buy tea direct from small factories and farmers, and see Kanchenjunga from Antu Danda without a crowd. Ilam is also known for its dairy and churpi cheese, large cardamom and the small round akabare chilli.

sections.heading: How to get there from India and Kathmandu
paras: From India, almost everyone enters at Kakarbhitta, opposite Panitanki on the Mechi River. Indian citizens need a passport or voter ID and no visa; Indian private cars need a customs pass at the border and are limited to 30 days per calendar year. From Kathmandu, fly to Bhadrapur and drive up the Mechi Highway. Shared jeeps and buses run between Birtamod, Fikkal and Ilam, but a private car with a local driver is far easier for families. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Kanyam, Ilam Bazaar, Mai Pokhari and Antu Danda
paras: Kanyam, at about 1,650 m on the Mechi Highway, is the garden most people picture: open, rolling slopes of clipped bushes with shade trees and paths for walking. It is about 2 hours from the border and an hour short of Ilam, so most visitors stop for an hour on the way up. Stay a night nearby for an empty garden at sunrise. Fikkal, a few kilometres on, is the market town for the area.

The Ilam Tea Estate wraps around the edge of Ilam Bazaar, a short walk from the hotels. A guided morning walk through the estate, followed by a tasting at a tea house in town, explains how first and second flush teas differ. The main factory opens to visitors only when management allows, so we do not promise a factory tour, but in the plucking season you can usually watch part of the process at a smaller unit.

Mai Pokhari is a sacred forest lake about 13 km from Ilam Bazaar, an hour by road, at about 2,100 m. It was listed as a Ramsar wetland in 2008, and its nine-cornered shoreline is surrounded by rhododendron and oak forest with a small temple. Festival days bring local pilgrims; on other days you may have the shore almost to yourself. Antu Danda, a ridge at 2,328 m in Shree Antu village on the India border, is the sunrise point: the sun comes up over the plains while Kanchenjunga turns pink to the north.

Shree Antu is home to Lepcha, Rai and Limbu families, and several run simple homestays a 15 to 30 minute walk from the view tower. Staying there means you leave your room at about 5 a.m. instead of driving up from Fikkal at 4 a.m. After sunrise, a path leads down through tea and cardamom fields towards Fikkal in 3–4 hours, mostly downhill, with tea stops in the villages on the way.

sections.heading: Tea seasons month by month
paras: Tea is plucked in Ilam from about March to November, and each flush tastes different. Visitors who want to see plucking should come between March and November; those who want the clearest Kanchenjunga views should come between October and February, when the bushes rest but the skies are sharpest. October and November give both, which makes them our favourite months.

sections.heading: Itineraries for two to five nights
paras: Ilam rewards slow travel, but even a short trip works because distances inside the district are short. These are the plans we use most often for travellers starting at the Kakarbhitta border or Bhadrapur.
list: 2 nights: Kanyam on the way up, one night in Ilam with an estate walk and Mai Pokhari, a pre-dawn drive to Antu Danda, and one night near Kanyam before returning to the border

4 nights, our 5-day tour from ₹22,000: two nights in Ilam for the estate, tea tasting, Mai Pokhari and a cardamom village, a homestay night at Shree Antu a short walk from the sunrise tower, and a final night near Kanyam
4–5 nights with Pathibhara: add a shared helicopter shuttle from Kanyam to Pathibhara Devi, about 30 minutes each way, on a clear morning; the road route via Phungling needs three extra nights
6–7 nights with Koshi Tappu: in winter, drive about 5–6 hours west to the wetland reserve for two nights of birding before flying home from Biratnagar

sections.heading: Where to stay and what it costs
paras: Hotels in Ilam Bazaar and Fikkal are simple, clean and family-run rather than luxury, with hot water and Nepali, Indian and some Chinese dishes. Homestays in Shree Antu and around the tea villages give twin rooms in family houses and home-cooked dal bhat, and save the 4 a.m. drive for sunrise. Rooms fill on Nepali and Indian holidays, especially Dashain, Tihar and the Durga Puja weeks, so book ahead.

Our 5-day tour starts from about ₹22,000 or US$260 per person for four travellers sharing a car and two twin rooms, from the Kakarbhitta border or Bhadrapur. A couple travelling alone pays about ₹31,000 each. Add about ₹2,500 per car for the Siliguri–border transfer. A Pathibhara helicopter seat from Kanyam adds about ₹22,000 per person at local shared rates.

sections.heading: Practical tips for an Ilam trip
paras: Ilam is easy, low and safe, with the highest point of a normal trip at Antu Danda, 2,328 m. A few practical details make it smoother.
list: Bring a warm jacket for sunrise at Antu Danda in every season; from December to February nights there can be close to freezing
Carry Nepali rupees for small shops and tea farmers; Indian ₹200 and ₹500 notes have been allowed since late 2025 within a ₹25,000 limit, but check current status before you travel
Buy tea from estate shops or farmer cooperatives in vacuum-sealed packs, which keep their flavour on the journey home
Avoid June to September if you want views: the monsoon brings cloud, leeches and landslides on the Mechi Highway
Ask before photographing pluckers at work, and stay on the paths between the rows so the bushes are not damaged
Vegetarian food is easy to find; tell us in advance about Jain or no onion and garlic meals

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Ilam?
faqs.a: Two nights is the minimum to see Kanyam, the Ilam Bazaar estate, Mai Pokhari and sunrise at Antu Danda without rushing. Four nights, as in our 5-day tour, adds a cardamom village, a homestay at Shree Antu and a slow last evening at Kanyam. Add a night for a Pathibhara helicopter darshan.

faqs.q: How far is Ilam from Siliguri?
faqs.a: About 130 km, which takes 4–4.5 hours including border formalities. Drive about an hour from Siliguri to the Panitanki–Kakarbhitta border, then about 95 km and 3–3.5 hours via Charali, Kanyam and Fikkal on the Mechi Highway. Bagdogra airport is a similar distance, about 4 hours from Ilam.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Ilam tea gardens?
faqs.a: October and November give clear Kanchenjunga views and autumn plucking together. March to May brings the first flush and spring flowers, with some afternoon haze. December to February has the sharpest views but bushes are resting. June to September is monsoon, with rain, cloud, leeches and landslides on the hill roads.

It is different rather than better. Darjeeling has the toy train, colonial hotels and more shops; Ilam is quieter, cheaper and less developed, with open gardens you can walk freely and very few tourist crowds. The two sit on the same ridges, so tea and views are similar. Ilam suits travellers who want peace over sightseeing lists.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Ilam?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings. The best viewpoint is Antu Danda at 2,328 m, about 1.5–2 hours from Ilam Bazaar, where Kanchenjunga turns pink at sunrise. Views are most reliable from October to February. From March onwards, haze and cloud often hide the mountains by mid-morning, so go early.

faqs.q: Do Indian tourists need a passport for Ilam?
faqs.a: No passport is needed. Indian citizens can enter Nepal at Kakarbhitta with either a passport or a voter ID card, and no visa is required. Children should carry a birth certificate or school ID. No special permit is needed for Ilam, Kanyam, Mai Pokhari or Antu Danda.

faqs.q: Can we visit an Ilam tea factory?
faqs.a: Sometimes. The main Ilam Tea Estate factory admits visitors only when management allows, so we never promise it. In the plucking season, from March to November, smaller factories and farmer units often let you watch withering, rolling and drying, and tea houses in the bazaar offer tastings of several grades.

faqs.q: Is the Ilam trip suitable for seniors and children?
faqs.a: Yes. Drives inside the district are 1–3 hours, walks are short and gentle, and the highest point, Antu Danda, is only 2,328 m, so altitude is not a concern. The only early start is the sunrise trip. Bring warm layers, because mornings at Antu and Kanyam are cold from November to February.

faqs.q: How much does an Ilam tour package cost?
faqs.a: Our 5-day Ilam tea gardens tour starts from about ₹22,000 or US$260 per person for four travellers sharing a car and two twin rooms, from the Kakarbhitta border or Bhadrapur. A couple pays about ₹31,000 each. The price includes four nights' stay, a private car, a local guide, tastings and most meals.
